title: TypeScript: Zero to Interview
subtitle: An 8-month, week-by-week course from your very first line of code to interview-ready — DSA solved in TypeScript and deep type-system mastery. Every week has a goal, lessons that never outrun what you've learned, and a capstone project.

weeks.goal: Write a program that prints text and does arithmetic with named values.
weeks.summary:
Welcome! This is the very beginning — no prior coding needed. This week you'll
run your first TypeScript program, print things to the screen, store values in
named variables, and do some arithmetic. That's genuinely all a lot of programs
do: take some values, combine them, and print a result.

Everything you write here runs and is **checked instantly**. Replace the
`____` in each drill with the missing piece, then press **Check**.

lessons.title: Your first program
lessons.lesson:
A **program** is a list of instructions the computer runs top to bottom. The
instruction you'll use most is `console.log(...)`, which prints its argument
followed by a newline.

```ts
console.log("Hello, world!");
```

Text wrapped in quotes is called a **string**. `console.log` can print strings,
numbers, and more. Every statement ends with a semicolon `;`.

exercises.title: Print a greeting
exercises.prompt: Make the program print exactly: Hello, world!
exercises.hint: A string is text in double quotes.
exercises.starter: console.log(____);
exercises.solution: console.log("Hello, world!");

exercises.title: Print two lines
exercises.prompt: Print two lines: first `Line one`, then `Line two`.
exercises.hint: Each console.log prints its own line.
exercises.starter:
console.log("Line one");
console.log(____);
exercises.solution:
console.log("Line one");
console.log("Line two");

quiz.question: What does console.log do?
options: Prints its argument, then a newline
quiz.explanation: console.log writes its argument to the output followed by a newline.

quiz.question: Which of these is a string?
quiz.explanation: A string is text wrapped in quotes, like "cat".

lessons.title: Variables: let and const
lessons.what: Naming values so you can reuse them.
lessons.lesson:
A **variable** is a named box for a value. Declare one with `const` (the name
keeps one value for good) or `let` (you can reassign it later). Prefer `const`
unless you truly need to change the value.

```ts
const name = "Ada";
let count = 0;
count = count + 1;
console.log(name);   // Ada
console.log(count);  // 1
```

Both are **block-scoped**: they exist only inside the `{ }` they're declared in.

exercises.title: Name a value
exercises.prompt: Store the string `Ada` in `name`, so the program prints `Hello, Ada`.
exercises.hint: Joining strings with + is called concatenation.
exercises.starter:
const name = ____;
console.log("Hello, " + name);
exercises.solution:
const name = "Ada";
console.log("Hello, " + name);

exercises.title: Reassign with let
exercises.prompt: Reassign `count` to 2 so the program prints 2.
exercises.hint: Reassignment is `count = 2;` — no `let` the second time.

lessons.title: Numbers & arithmetic
lessons.lesson:
TypeScript has one `number` type for whole numbers and decimals alike. The
operators are `+` `-` `*` `/` and `%` (remainder — what's left after division).

```ts
console.log(6 * 7);    // 42
console.log(17 % 5);   // 2  (17 = 3*5 + 2)
console.log(10 / 4);   // 2.5
```

exercises.title: Multiply
exercises.prompt: Print the product of `a` and `b` (should be 42).
exercises.hint: Use the * operator.

exercises.title: Remainder
exercises.prompt: Print the remainder of `total` divided by 5.
exercises.hint: `%` gives the remainder.
exercises.starter:
const total = 17;
console.log(____);
exercises.solution:
const total = 17;
console.log(total % 5);

capstone.title: Receipt printer
capstone.brief:
Put Week 1 together. Using only `const`, arithmetic, and string joining, print a
two-line receipt for **4 coffees at $3 each**:

```
Coffee x4
Total: $12
```

The scaffold declares the item, price, and quantity. Fill in the calculation and
the two `console.log` lines.

exercise.title: Receipt printer
exercise.prompt: Print the item line and the total line exactly as shown.
exercise.hint: total is price * qty; build each line by joining strings with +.

weeks.goal: Read input from the user and build text with template literals and string tools.

lessons.title: Reading input
lessons.lesson:
Reading input is boilerplate you'll reuse constantly. Read it all, trim it, and
you have a string to work with.

```ts
import * as fs from "fs";
const line = fs.readFileSync(0, "utf8").trim();
console.log(line);   // echoes what was typed
```

exercises.title: Echo the input
exercises.prompt: Read the whole input (trimmed) and print it back.
exercises.hint: readFileSync(0, "utf8") reads stdin; .trim() drops surrounding whitespace.

exercises.title: Greet the input
exercises.prompt: Read a name and print `Hello, <name>!`.
exercises.hint: Join the pieces with +.

quiz.question: Why call .trim() on the input?
options: To remove the trailing newline and stray spaces
To convert it to a number
quiz.explanation: Input usually ends in a newline; .trim() removes surrounding whitespace.

quiz.question: What type does fs.readFileSync(0, "utf8") return?
quiz.explanation: With the "utf8" encoding it returns the input as a string.

lessons.title: Template literals
lessons.what: Splicing values into text with backticks.
lessons.lesson:
Backtick strings let you drop values straight into text with `${ }` — much
clearer than gluing pieces with `+`.

```ts
const name = "Sam";
const age = 3;
console.log(`Hi ${name}, you are ${age}`);   // Hi Sam, you are 3
console.log(`2 + 2 = ${2 + 2}`);              // 2 + 2 = 4
```

exercises.title: Welcome message
exercises.prompt: Use a template literal to print `Hi <name>, welcome!`.
exercises.hint: Use backticks and ${name}.

exercises.title: Inline arithmetic
exercises.prompt: Print `<a> + <b> = <sum>` using a template literal.
exercises.hint: You can put an expression like a + b inside ${ }.

lessons.title: String methods
lessons.lesson:
Strings come with handy built-in methods:

```ts
const s = "hello";
console.log(s.length);         // 5   (a property, no parentheses)
console.log(s.toUpperCase());  // HELLO
console.log(s.includes("ell")); // true
console.log(s.slice(0, 3));    // hel
```

exercises.title: Shout it
exercises.prompt: Print the input in UPPERCASE.
exercises.hint: Call .toUpperCase() on the string.

exercises.title: Count the letters
exercises.prompt: Print how many characters the input has.
exercises.hint: length is a property — no parentheses.

capstone.title: Name card
capstone.brief:
Read a single name and print a three-line card:

```
Name: Ada
Letters: 3
Shout: ADA
```

Use a template literal for each line, plus `.length` and `.toUpperCase()`.

exercise.title: Name card
exercise.prompt: Print the three lines exactly, based on the input name.

weeks.goal: Branch on conditions with if/else and combine tests with boolean logic.
weeks.summary:
Programs get interesting when they **choose** what to do. This week: comparisons
that produce `true`/`false`, `if`/`else` branching, and the logical operators
`&&` (and), `||` (or), `!` (not).

One new helper you'll need: input arrives as **text**, so wrap it in `Number(...)`
when you want to do math or numeric comparisons:

```ts
const n = Number(fs.readFileSync(0, "utf8").trim());  // "42" -> 42
```

lessons.title: Booleans & comparison
lessons.what: Values that are true or false.
lessons.lesson:
Comparisons produce a **boolean** (`true` or `false`). Always compare with
`===` / `!==` (strict — no surprise conversions), plus `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`.

```ts
console.log(5 > 3);        // true
console.log("a" === "b");  // false
console.log(10 >= 10);     // true
```

exercises.title: Greater than ten
exercises.prompt: Print whether the number is greater than 10.
exercises.hint: Use the > operator; console.log prints true/false.

exercises.title: Exact match
exercises.prompt: Print whether the input equals the string `yes`.
exercises.hint: Use === for a strict comparison.

quiz.question: Which operator should you use to compare for equality?
quiz.explanation: === is strict equality (no type coercion). = is assignment.

quiz.question: What does Number("7") produce?
quiz.explanation: Number(...) converts a numeric string into a number.

lessons.title: if / else

exercises.title: Sign of a number
exercises.prompt: Print `non-negative` when n >= 0, otherwise `negative`.
exercises.hint: Zero counts as non-negative, so use >=.

exercises.title: Letter grade
exercises.prompt: Fill the middle test so 85 prints B (>=80), 95 prints A, 70 prints C.
exercises.hint: The B branch is for scores of 80 or more.

lessons.title: Logical operators
lessons.lesson:
- `a && b` is true only when **both** are true.
- `a || b` is true when **either** is true.
- `!a` flips a boolean.

```ts
console.log(n >= 1 && n <= 5);   // in range 1..5 ?
console.log(s === "y" || s === "yes");
```

exercises.title: In range
exercises.prompt: Print whether n is between 1 and 5 (inclusive).
exercises.hint: Both conditions must hold, so use &&.

exercises.title: Yes in either form
exercises.prompt: Print true when the input is `y` or `yes`.
exercises.hint: Either spelling is acceptable, so use ||.

capstone.title: Ticket pricing
capstone.brief:
Read a person's **age** and print their ticket price:

- under 5 → `Free`
- 5 to 17 → `$10`
- 65 and over → `$12`
- everyone else → `$20`

Fill in the `if`/`else if`/`else` chain.

exercise.title: Ticket pricing
exercise.prompt: Print the correct price for the given age.
exercise.hint: Order matters — test the youngest and oldest bands with the right cutoffs.

weeks.goal: Repeat work with while and for loops, and accumulate results.
weeks.summary:
Computers shine at doing the same thing many times. This week you'll meet
`while` and `for` loops, the idea of an **accumulator** (a running total or
counter), and `for...of` for walking through text a character at a time.

lessons.title: while loops

exercises.title: Sum 1..n
exercises.prompt: Loop while i <= n, adding each i to sum. Print the total.
exercises.hint: Keep going while i has not passed n.

exercises.title: Countdown
exercises.prompt: Print n, n-1, ... down to 1, each on its own line.
exercises.hint: Move i toward 0 each pass so the loop ends.

quiz.question: What is an 'accumulator'?
options: A variable that builds up a result across iterations
quiz.explanation: An accumulator (like a running sum or counter) collects a result as the loop runs.

quiz.question: What happens if a while loop's condition never becomes false?
quiz.explanation: Without progress toward ending, the loop runs forever (an infinite loop).

lessons.title: for loops

exercises.title: Factorial
exercises.prompt: Multiply 1*2*...*n into product. Print it.
exercises.hint: Each pass multiplies the running product by i.

exercises.title: Count evens
exercises.prompt: Count how many numbers from 1..10 are even. Print the count.
exercises.hint: A number is even when its remainder mod 2 is 0.

lessons.title: Looping over text
lessons.what: for...of walks a string character by character.

exercises.title: Count a letter
exercises.prompt: Count how many times the letter `a` appears in the input.
exercises.hint: Compare each character to "a".

exercises.title: Reverse a string
exercises.prompt: Build the input backwards by putting each new char in front.
exercises.hint: Prepend each character: ch + out.

capstone.title: FizzBuzz
capstone.brief:
The classic. Read a number **n** and print the numbers `1` to `n`, one per line,
with two twists:

- multiples of 3 → `Fizz`
- multiples of 5 → `Buzz`
- multiples of both → `FizzBuzz`

Fill in the loop body (test the both-case first!).

exercise.title: FizzBuzz
exercise.prompt: Print 1..n applying the Fizz / Buzz / FizzBuzz rules.
exercise.hint: Check divisibility by 15 before 3 and 5, or the both-case never fires.

tests.output:
1
2
Fizz
4
Buzz
Fizz
7
8
Fizz
Buzz
11
Fizz
13
14
FizzBuzz

weeks.goal: Package logic into reusable functions with parameters and return values.
weeks.summary:
A **function** is a named, reusable piece of logic: give it inputs
(**parameters**), it hands back a result (**return value**). Functions let you
name an idea once and use it everywhere. This week: declaring functions, arrow
functions, and returning values.

You'll see type annotations like `(x: number): number` — they document what goes
in and comes out. (They're checked while you write, then stripped before the
program runs.)

lessons.title: Declaring functions

exercises.title: Square
exercises.prompt: Return x times itself.
exercises.hint: Multiply x by x.

exercises.title: Greet
exercises.prompt: Return a greeting string for the given name.
exercises.hint: Return a template literal using name.

quiz.question: What does `return` do?
options: Sends a value back to the caller and ends the function
quiz.explanation: return produces the function's result and stops its execution.

quiz.question: In `function f(x: number)`, what is `x`?
options: A parameter (an input to the function)
quiz.explanation: x is a parameter — a named input the caller supplies.

lessons.title: Parameters & return values
lessons.what: Passing inputs and using the result.

exercises.title: Double the input
exercises.prompt: Return x doubled, then print double(n) for the input n.
exercises.hint: Multiply the parameter by 2.

exercises.title: Absolute value
exercises.prompt: Return the negation of x when x is negative.
exercises.hint: The opposite of x is -x.

lessons.title: Arrow functions
lessons.what: A shorter way to write small functions.
lessons.lesson:
Arrow functions are compact. When the body is a single expression, its value is
returned automatically (no `return` needed).

```ts
const cube = (x: number): number => x * x * x;
console.log(cube(3));   // 27
```

exercises.title: Cube (arrow)
exercises.prompt: Return x cubed from the arrow function.
exercises.hint: x times x times x.
exercises.starter:
const cube = (x: number): number => ____;
console.log(cube(3));
exercises.solution:
const cube = (x: number): number => x * x * x;
console.log(cube(3));

exercises.title: Triple (arrow)
exercises.prompt: Return x * 3, then print triple(n) for the input.
exercises.hint: Multiply x by 3.

capstone.title: Temperature converter
capstone.brief:
Write two functions and use them together. Read a Celsius temperature and print:

1. that temperature in Fahrenheit (`C * 9 / 5 + 32`)
2. the result converted back to Celsius (`(F - 32) * 5 / 9`) — which should equal
   what you started with

For input `100`:

```
212
100
```

exercise.title: Temperature converter
exercise.prompt: Fill in the two function bodies.
exercise.hint: cToF is c*9/5+32; fToC reverses it with (f-32)*5/9.

weeks.goal: Store lists of values and process them with loops and array methods.
weeks.summary:
An **array** holds an ordered list of values, reached by index (`nums[0]` is the
first). This week: creating and indexing arrays, iterating them, and the trio
`map` / `filter` / `reduce` that makes list-processing concise.

To read a line of numbers into an array:

```ts
const nums = fs.readFileSync(0, "utf8").trim().split(" ").map(Number);
```

`.split(" ")` cuts the text into pieces at spaces; `.map(Number)` turns each
piece into a number.

lessons.title: Creating & indexing
lessons.lesson:
```ts
const names = ["Ada", "Bo", "Cy"];
console.log(names[0]);      // Ada   (indexes start at 0)
console.log(names.length);  // 3
```

exercises.title: First number
exercises.prompt: Read the numbers and print the first one.
exercises.hint: The first element is at index 0.

exercises.title: How many
exercises.prompt: Print how many space-separated words the input has.
exercises.hint: length gives the number of elements.

quiz.question: What index is the first element of an array?
quiz.explanation: Arrays are zero-indexed: the first element is at index 0.

quiz.question: What does "3 5 7".split(" ") produce?
quiz.explanation: split cuts the string at each space into an array of pieces.

lessons.title: Iterating & accumulating

exercises.title: Sum the list
exercises.prompt: Add every number and print the total.
exercises.hint: Add each x to the running sum.

exercises.title: Largest
exercises.prompt: Track and print the largest number in the list.
exercises.hint: Replace best whenever x is bigger.

lessons.title: map, filter, reduce
lessons.lesson:
- `map` makes a new array by transforming each element.
- `filter` keeps only elements that pass a test.
- `join` glues an array back into a string.

```ts
const nums = [1, 2, 3];
console.log(nums.map((x) => x * 2).join(" "));   // 2 4 6
console.log(nums.filter((x) => x % 2 === 1).length); // 2
```

exercises.title: Count evens
exercises.prompt: Keep the even numbers and print how many there are.
exercises.hint: Even means remainder 0 mod 2.

exercises.title: Double them
exercises.prompt: Double every number and print them space-separated.
exercises.hint: map transforms each x to x * 2.

capstone.title: Number stats
capstone.brief:
Read a line of numbers and print three stats:

```
sum 14
max 5
count 5
```

for input `3 1 4 1 5`. Fill in the loop that computes the sum and max, then the
three report lines.

exercise.title: Number stats
exercise.prompt: Compute sum and max in one pass, then print the report.
exercise.hint: Start max at nums[0], then update sum and max together in one loop.

weeks.goal: Model structured data with objects, and combine them with arrays.
weeks.summary:
An **object** groups related values under named keys — perfect for modeling a
'thing' like a user or a product. This week: object literals, reading and
updating properties, and arrays of objects (the shape of most real data).

```ts
const user = { name: "Ada", age: 36 };
console.log(user.name);   // Ada
user.age = user.age + 1;  // update a property
```

lessons.title: Object basics
lessons.lesson:
Reach a property with dot notation: `obj.key`. You can read it or, on a `const`
object, still change its properties.

```ts
const point = { x: 3, y: 4 };
console.log(point.x);        // 3
point.y = point.y + 1;       // 5
```

exercises.title: Read a property
exercises.prompt: Print the user's name.
exercises.hint: Access it with user.name.
exercises.starter:
const user = { name: "Ada", age: 36 };
console.log(____);
exercises.solution:
const user = { name: "Ada", age: 36 };
console.log(user.name);

exercises.title: Update a property
exercises.prompt: Add 5 to counter.value, then print it.
exercises.hint: Read the current value and add 5.

quiz.question: How do you read the `name` property of `user`?
An object is best for...
options: Grouping related values under named keys
quiz.explanation: Objects group related fields (name, age, ...) under keys.

lessons.title: Objects & functions

exercises.title: Full name
exercises.prompt: Return the first and last name joined by a space.
exercises.hint: Template literal with p.first and p.last.

exercises.title: Build from input
exercises.prompt: Store a greeting on the object, then print it.
exercises.hint: The greeting is a template literal using name.

lessons.title: Arrays of objects

exercises.title: Total ages
exercises.prompt: Sum everyone's age and print it.
exercises.hint: Add each person's age to total.

exercises.title: Count adults
exercises.prompt: Count people aged 21 or older and print the count.
exercises.hint: Keep people whose age is at least 21.

capstone.title: Design: a tiny library catalog
capstone.brief:
A **free-build** project (no auto-grader — build it your way, then mark the week
done). In the editor, model a small **library**:

1. Represent each book as an object with `title`, `author`, and `available`
   (a boolean).
2. Put several books in an array.
3. Write a function that takes the array and prints a report: how many books
   there are, and the titles of the ones currently available.

Try to use everything from Weeks 1–7: variables, loops, functions, arrays, and
objects. There's no single right answer — experiment. When you're happy with the
output, click **Mark done**.

weeks.goal: Annotate values and name shapes with type aliases and interfaces.
weeks.summary:
You've used TypeScript's types implicitly all along. This week you make them
explicit: **annotations** on values and functions, and naming reusable shapes
with **`interface`** and **`type`**. Well-named types are documentation the
compiler checks for you.

Remember: types are erased before the program runs, so the drills still exercise
runtime logic — the annotations are there to describe it.

lessons.title: Annotations & inference
lessons.what: Writing types on values and functions.

exercises.title: Typed total
exercises.prompt: Compute price * qty into the annotated total.
exercises.hint: Multiply the two annotated numbers.

exercises.title: Typed repeat
exercises.prompt: Return the string repeated n times.
exercises.hint: Strings have a .repeat(n) method.

quiz.question: What happens to type annotations when the program runs?
options: They are stripped away — types are compile-time only
quiz.explanation: TypeScript types are erased before execution; they guide you and the compiler, not the runtime.

quiz.question: What does `interface` do?
options: Names the shape of an object type
quiz.explanation: An interface names a reusable object shape (its properties and their types).

lessons.title: Interfaces & type aliases
lessons.what: Naming the shape of your data.

exercises.title: Manhattan distance
exercises.prompt: Return |p.x| + |p.y| using Math.abs.
exercises.hint: Add the absolute values of x and y.

exercises.title: Labelled user
exercises.prompt: Return `<name> (admin)` when admin is true, else just the name.
exercises.hint: A ternary `cond ? a : b` picks a when cond is true.

lessons.title: Typed arrays of records
lessons.what: Putting interfaces to work over lists.

exercises.title: Total price
exercises.prompt: Reduce the items to the sum of their prices.
exercises.hint: Each step adds it.price to the running sum.

capstone.title: Typed contacts report
capstone.brief:
Model a contact list with an `interface`, then report on it. Given three
contacts, print:

```
Total: 3
Adults: 2
Names: Ada, Bo, Cy
```

(Adults are aged 18+.) Fill in the block that computes the adults, the two
counts, and the comma-joined names.

exercise.title: Typed contacts report
exercise.prompt: Use filter, map, join and .length over a typed array of records.
exercise.hint: filter for age>=18, map to names then join with ", ".

tests.output:
Total: 3
Adults: 2
Names: Ada, Bo, Cy

weeks.goal: Model a value that's 'one of several' and narrow it safely before use.
Write functions and types that work over any type without losing safety.
Lock data down with readonly, as const, and pure (copy-don't-mutate) updates.
Reshape existing types with Partial, Pick, Omit, and Record.
Handle possibly-missing values with ?., ??, and strict null checks.
Fail loudly and recover gracefully with try/catch and the Result pattern.
Split a program across files with import/export and clear boundaries.
Work with promises and async/await for tasks that take time.
Build and use LIFO/FIFO structures and know when each fits.
Reach for hash maps and sets to get O(1) lookup and de-duplication.
Solve problems whose definition refers to themselves.
Model data as nodes that point to other nodes.
Reason about the time and space cost of your code.
Binary search a sorted array and sweep it with two pointers.
Answer range and subarray questions in linear time.
Understand the common sorts and use sorting as a problem-solving tool.
Generate and search combinatorial spaces (subsets, permutations).
Turn overlapping recursion into fast, memoized DP.
Traverse graphs and grids to answer reachability and shortest-path questions.
Use priority queues and interval techniques on classic problems.
Compute new types from existing ones with conditional and mapped types.
Bend the inference engine and build types from string patterns.
Solve 'type gymnastics' puzzles the way interviewers pose them.
Put it together under time: DSA solved in TypeScript plus type challenges.
